questions.stem: Which feature best distinguishes a service from a good?
options: it can be stored in a warehouse until a customer is ready to buy it
it is only ever provided by government agencies, not by businesses
it is intangible and usually produced and consumed at the same time
it is always sold at a lower price than a physical product would be
questions.explanation: Services, such as a haircut or legal advice, cannot be touched or stored and are usually consumed as they are produced. Storing items until sale is a feature of goods.

questions.stem: A Dubbo bakery sells bread and cakes and also runs weekend cake-decorating classes. Which statement is correct?
options: the bread and cakes are goods and the classes are a service
the bread, cakes and classes are all goods sold by the bakery
the classes are goods because customers take home a decorated cake
the bread and cakes are services because they are made by staff
questions.explanation: Bread and cakes are tangible products, so they are goods; a class is an intangible experience delivered by the baker, so it is a service. Taking something home from a class does not turn the teaching into a good.

questions.stem: In business, revenue is:
options: the money spent on wages, rent and materials
the money the owners first put into the business
the money earned from selling goods and services
the money left after all expenses have been paid
questions.explanation: Revenue is income from sales, before any costs are deducted. The amount left after expenses is profit, and money the owners invest is capital.

questions.stem: A Newcastle cafe sells 4,000 coffees in a month at $5 each. Its total costs for the month are $14,500. What is its profit for the month?
questions.explanation: Revenue = 4,000 x $5 = $20,000, and profit = revenue - costs = $20,000 - $14,500 = $5,500. $20,000 is revenue, not profit.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a fixed cost for a small manufacturer?
options: the freight paid on each order
the monthly rent on its factory
the raw materials for each unit
the packaging used for each item
questions.explanation: Fixed costs, such as rent, stay the same whatever the level of output. Materials, packaging and freight per order are variable costs because they rise as more is produced and sold.

questions.stem: A Penrith business has fixed costs of $6,000 a month and variable costs of $4 per unit. It sells 2,000 units a month at $9 each. What is its monthly profit?
questions.explanation: Revenue = 2,000 x $9 = $18,000. Total costs = $6,000 + (2,000 x $4) = $14,000, so profit = $4,000. Ignoring fixed costs gives $10,000.

questions.stem: A Wagga Wagga retailer's revenue rose from $200,000 to $220,000, but its profit fell from $30,000 to $20,000. Which explanation is correct?
options: its total costs fell by $10,000 while revenue was rising
its profit is calculated before any costs are deducted
its total costs rose by $30,000, more than the rise in revenue
its revenue must really have fallen, because profit always follows revenue
questions.explanation: Costs = revenue - profit, so costs rose from $170,000 to $200,000, an increase of $30,000, outstripping the $20,000 rise in revenue. Higher revenue does not guarantee higher profit.

questions.stem: The transformation process in a business is best described as:
options: converting customer complaints into new policies
converting inputs into outputs of goods or services
converting profits into dividends paid to the owners
converting a sole trader into a registered company
questions.explanation: Every business transforms inputs, such as materials, labour, information and equipment, into outputs that customers want. The other changes are financial or legal, not the transformation process.

questions.stem: A Mudgee winery crushes grapes, ferments the juice, ages the wine and bottles it. In the transformation process, the fermenting and ageing are:
options: the outputs that the winery sells to customers
the feedback received from wine customers
the processes that turn inputs into the output
the inputs that the winery buys from growers
questions.explanation: Grapes, labour and equipment are inputs, the bottled wine is the output, and the steps in between, such as fermenting and ageing, are the transformation processes.

questions.stem: A Sydney accounting firm uses its staff's skills, clients' records and software to prepare tax returns. Which statement about its transformation process is correct?
options: service businesses transform inputs such as skills and information into outputs
service businesses have no transformation process because nothing physical is made
the clients' records are the firm's output because they are returned to clients
the software is the output because it produces the finished tax returns
questions.explanation: Service firms also transform inputs, here staff time, expertise, information and technology, into an output, the completed tax return. A physical product is not needed for a transformation process.

questions.stem: A business creates value when:
options: it buys its inputs at the highest price offered by suppliers
it reduces its outputs so that fewer goods are left unsold
customers value its outputs more than the cost of the inputs used
it sells its outputs for exactly what its inputs cost it to buy from suppliers
questions.explanation: Value is created when the transformation process produces something customers will pay more for than the inputs cost. Selling at the cost of inputs adds no value and leaves no profit.

questions.stem: A Hunter Valley farm sells fresh tomatoes for $4 per kilogram. It begins making tomato relish, which sells for $24 per kilogram of tomatoes used, while extra costs add $8. Which conclusion is most valid?
options: further processing adds value only if the selling price of tomatoes rises
further processing adds value because the extra revenue exceeds the extra cost
further processing destroys value because the relish needs extra ingredients
further processing adds no value, because the tomatoes are the same input either way
questions.explanation: Each kilogram now earns $24 instead of $4, an extra $20, for only $8 of extra cost, so the transformation adds $12 of value per kilogram. Extra costs reduce value only if they exceed the extra revenue.

questions.stem: In ABS business statistics, a small business is one that employs:
options: fewer than 100 people
fewer than 50 people
fewer than 20 people
fewer than 200 people
questions.explanation: The ABS counts businesses employing 0 to 19 people as small, 20 to 199 as medium and 200 or more as large. Fewer than 200 is the upper limit for medium businesses.

questions.stem: Using ABS employment size ranges, a Tamworth engineering firm with 85 employees is classified as:
options: a large business
a micro business
a medium business
a small business
questions.explanation: Medium businesses employ 20 to 199 people, so 85 employees is medium. Small means fewer than 20 and large means 200 or more.

questions.stem: Which business operates in the primary industry?
options: a steel mill in Port Kembla
a bank branch in Orange
a bakery in Coffs Harbour
a wheat farm near Moree
questions.explanation: Primary industry businesses extract or grow natural resources, as in farming, fishing, forestry and mining. A steel mill and bakery make products (secondary), and a bank provides services (tertiary).

questions.stem: A Lithgow business turns timber into kitchen cabinets. It belongs to the:
options: tertiary industry, because it sells to households
quaternary industry, because it designs cabinets
secondary industry, because it manufactures products
primary industry, because its main input is a natural resource
questions.explanation: Secondary industry businesses process raw materials into finished goods through manufacturing or construction. Using timber as an input does not make it primary; the forestry business that cut the timber is primary.

questions.stem: A physiotherapy clinic in Bathurst is classified in the tertiary industry because it:
options: manufactures goods from materials
operates in more than one country
provides a service to customers
grows or extracts raw materials
questions.explanation: Tertiary industry businesses provide services such as health, retail, finance and tourism. Extracting materials is primary and manufacturing is secondary.

questions.stem: Classified by geographic reach, a business with production and sales operations in several countries is:
options: a global business
a local business
a national business
a state-based business
questions.explanation: Geographic reach describes where a business operates: local businesses serve one area, national businesses operate across Australia, and global businesses operate in many countries.

questions.stem: A Byron Bay surf brand has 12 employees and one shop but sells online to customers in 30 countries. Which classification is correct?
options: small in size but global in geographic reach
large in size, because it sells to customers worldwide
medium in size because it trades overseas
local in reach because it has only one shop
questions.explanation: Size is measured by employees (12 is small), while geographic reach is measured by where customers and operations are. Online selling lets a small business reach global markets, so the two classifications are independent.

questions.stem: The operations function of a business is mainly responsible for:
options: producing the goods or services the business sells
recruiting, training and paying the business's staff
obtaining funds and monitoring the financial position
researching customers and promoting the products
questions.explanation: Operations manages the transformation process that turns inputs into goods and services. The other roles belong to human resources, finance and marketing.

questions.stem: Which task belongs to the finance function?
options: preparing budgets and monitoring cash flow
designing the layout of the factory floor and its workstations
running an advertising campaign online
conducting interviews for new staff
questions.explanation: The finance function plans, obtains and controls the business's money, including budgets and cash flow. Factory layout is operations, advertising is marketing and interviews are human resources.

questions.stem: A Gosford business is opening a second store and needs to hire and train 15 new staff. Which business function leads this task?
options: human resources
operations
marketing
finance
questions.explanation: Human resources manages the employment cycle, including recruitment, selection, training and development. Finance will fund the wages, but hiring and training are HR roles.

questions.stem: Marketing at an Albury food company plans a national promotion expected to double orders. Which response shows the functions working interdependently?
options: operations plans extra output, finance funds it and HR arranges extra staff
marketing runs the promotion while the other functions wait to see the final results
finance cuts the budgets of operations and HR to pay for the promotion
operations keeps output steady so that inventory costs do not increase
questions.explanation: Business functions depend on each other: higher demand requires more production, funding and staff. If operations does not expand output, the promotion leads to stockouts and unhappy customers.

questions.stem: A Parramatta bakery chain aims to open five new stores in the next three years. This is mainly a:
options: growth goal
profit goal
social goal
environmental goal
questions.explanation: Growth goals aim to increase the size of the business, such as more stores, more sales or a larger market share. A profit goal concerns the surplus of revenue over costs.

questions.stem: A Sydney software firm sets a goal of launching two new apps each year based on ideas from its staff. This is mainly:
options: a profit goal
a social goal
an innovation goal
a growth goal
questions.explanation: Innovation goals aim to create new or improved products and processes. Successful new apps may later support growth and profit, but the goal itself is about innovating.

questions.stem: A Wollongong manufacturer aims to send zero waste to landfill by 2030, while a Sydney cafe aims to employ 10 young people leaving out-of-home care. These goals are:
options: environmental and social respectively
social and environmental respectively
both profit goals in the long term
both growth goals for the businesses
questions.explanation: Cutting landfill waste is an environmental outcome, while giving jobs to disadvantaged young people is a social outcome. Neither goal is mainly about profit or size.

questions.stem: A Tweed Heads business switches to recycled packaging that costs 15 per cent more than its old packaging. Which tension between goals does this show?
options: an environmental goal may reduce profit in the short term
a growth goal always reduces the business's innovation
a social goal always increases the business's profit
a profit goal requires using the cheapest packaging by law
questions.explanation: Pursuing environmental outcomes can raise costs and lower short-term profit, though it may build reputation and customer loyalty over time. Goals can conflict, so managers must balance them.

questions.stem: A profit goal for a business aims to:
options: maximise the number of stores the business opens
maximise the amount by which revenue exceeds costs
maximise the number of people the business employs
maximise the number of products the business sells
questions.explanation: Profit is revenue minus costs, and profit goals focus on that surplus. Selling more products or opening stores are growth measures that do not guarantee higher profit.

questions.stem: An entrepreneur is best described as a person who:
options: identifies an opportunity and takes the risk of starting a business
manages one department of a large company on behalf of its owners
lends money to a business in exchange for regular interest payments
supplies raw materials to businesses under a long-term contract
questions.explanation: Entrepreneurs spot opportunities, organise resources and bear the risk of a new venture in the hope of reward. Managing a department for others is a manager's role, and lending is a creditor's.

questions.stem: Which best describes the relationship between a business and the government as a stakeholder?
options: government owns a share of every private business and receives part of its profit
government chooses the prices that private businesses charge for most products
government has no relationship with a business at all unless the business breaks the law
government sets laws and collects taxes, and businesses provide jobs and tax revenue
questions.explanation: Governments regulate businesses, collect taxes and provide infrastructure, while businesses provide employment, goods and tax revenue. Most private businesses set their own prices.

questions.stem: A Lismore hardware store pays its main supplier on time and shares sales forecasts with it. The supplier gives priority delivery during shortages. This shows that:
options: the supplier has become an owner of the hardware store
suppliers are internal stakeholders of every business
good supplier relationships benefit both the business and the supplier
suppliers are interested mainly in the dividends that the business pays its owners
questions.explanation: Suppliers want reliable payment and steady orders; in return they offer dependable supply and support. Suppliers are external stakeholders, not owners.

questions.stem: In a large listed company, shareholders want higher dividends, but managers want to spend profits on expansion that raises their own status and pay. This illustrates:
options: that expansion cannot be funded from a company's retained profits
the separation of ownership and management, which can cause conflicting interests
that managers and owners are always the same people in a listed company
that shareholders are not stakeholders because they do not work there
questions.explanation: In large companies, owners (shareholders) appoint managers to run the business, and the two groups' interests may differ. In a small sole trader business, owner and manager are usually the same person.

questions.stem: Customers are stakeholders whose main interest in a business is usually:
options: regular orders and prompt payment of invoices
dividends and growth in the value of shares
quality products at a fair price with good service
job security and safe working conditions
questions.explanation: Customers want value: quality, fair prices and reliable service. Job security is an employee interest, prompt payment a supplier interest and dividends an owner interest.

questions.stem: Why is corporate social responsibility (CSR) important to many businesses?
options: it guarantees the business higher profits in every year
it removes the need to consider shareholders' interests
it builds trust and reputation with customers, employees and the community
it allows the business to ignore laws it considers too costly
questions.explanation: Acting responsibly can strengthen reputation, customer loyalty and staff attraction and reduce the risk of conflict with the community. It does not override the law or guarantee profit.

questions.stem: Which action by a Newcastle manufacturer best demonstrates CSR rather than legal compliance?
options: paying its employees the minimum wages required under their award
lodging its tax returns with the ATO by the required due date
holding the licence required to discharge waste into the sewer
voluntarily funding a local river clean-up and publishing its emissions
questions.explanation: CSR means going beyond what the law requires to act in the interests of society and the environment. Paying award wages, lodging tax returns and holding licences are legal obligations.

questions.stem: A social enterprise is a business that:
options: is a charity that relies entirely on donations instead of selling anything
distributes all of its profits to private shareholders as dividends
trades to achieve a social or environmental purpose and reinvests most profits in it
is owned and run by the government to deliver essential public services
questions.explanation: Social enterprises sell goods or services like other businesses, but their main purpose is a social or environmental mission, and most profit goes back into that mission. Unlike many charities, they earn income from trading.

questions.stem: A Marrickville cafe is a social enterprise that trains refugees as baristas. Which statement about its stakeholders is most accurate?
options: its customers have no interest in its mission, because they only buy coffee
its trainees are not stakeholders, because they are not paid as permanent staff
its trainees are key beneficiaries, and customers may buy partly to support the mission
its only stakeholders are its owners, because social enterprises do not have customers
questions.explanation: Social enterprises have the usual stakeholders plus the people their mission serves. Customers and partners are often attracted by the mission, so the business must balance commercial success with social impact.
